memories.memory_text: I knelt down and held my handkerchief to Riley Delaney's nose—his face was all smeared with chocolate, and he tried to talk while I told him to blow. When he finally did, I said, 'There, I bet that feels better,' and he sniffed and said 'Yeah.'

I looked around at all those kids swarming the car and said, 'So many children. Are they all Elliot Vale?'—it just came out, I was overwhelmed, seeing so many little faces staring at us like we were something from another world.
I told Skyler Keaton I was two months pregnant, barely above a whisper—it felt so fragile saying it out loud, like it might break me.
I couldn't stop the words from spilling out—I told Skyler Keaton I couldn't have a baby while Logan Cavendish was going off to drop bombs on Mandalay, that I didn't even know if he'd come back.
When Logan Cavendish leaned in to hug me, I hit his chest—over and over—because he kept saying he'd come back like he actually knew that, like it was a promise he could keep.
I shook Skyler Keaton's hand and said, 'I guess I'll see you around the Maplewood Park. Thanks for everything.'
I whispered 'I love you, Logan Cavendish' as I walked toward him, the words slipping out quiet and true, just for him.
I took Drew Hayes by the shoulders and told her I had a ton of clothes that would fit her—she seemed to like that.
I teased Skyler Keaton, asking him how many women he's known, and he got all flustered and looked away—I could tell he didn’t want to answer, but he was smiling, so I knew he liked it.
After I joked about King Kong and medicine, I pushed him—just a quick, playful shove—and he was smiling, we were both laughing, it felt like we were closer than before.
I know this was right—I said it out loud, and I needed Skyler Keaton to hear it, even if he didn’t believe me.
I whispered that I told him too—just barely loud enough for Skyler Keaton to catch it, like I was afraid of what it meant.
I walked in and saw him moving his things around like he belonged there, and I said, 'So, you're staying,' even though Jesse Whitaker already told me—he could've told me himself.

I remember how Skyler Keaton just stared at me, his eyes full of something I’d never seen before—like looking at me actually hurt him. He said he’d seen everything in other women but felt nothing, and then with me, it *hurt* to look.
I remember sitting by the fire with Skyler Keaton and Jesse Whitaker, the game pieces between us, feeling like this—right here—was where I was supposed to be.
I was lying there, completely naked, heart pounding, after we were interrupted—I felt exposed and frozen, like I couldn’t move no matter how hard I tried.
I heard Finley Thorne’s voice—calm, almost gentle—saying we’d fallen in love, and something about not worrying… but his words didn’t comfort me, they just made everything feel heavier.

I was sitting beside Skyler Keaton in the dark, watching 'Rebecca' play out on the screen, just trying to stay close to him while that voice filled the theatre—so quiet, but so heavy, like it wasn't just part of the movie.
I laughed when the song changed and he started dancing like a fool, but I grabbed a pillow and hit him—just to mess with the moment, to push back at how fast everything fell apart.
After swinging pillows back and forth, I remember him pinning my arms—us both breathless—and even with that dumb music still playing, I kissed him hard, like I could bring the feeling back on my own.

I remember shouting at Skyler Keaton in Maplewood Park, my voice breaking as I told him I didn’t know if I wanted him or Logan Cavendish—I love him, I *do*, but I grew up with Logan Cavendish and that doesn’t just go away.
I said it so bitterly—I don’t even know if I meant to hurt him—but I remember the sharpness in my voice when I said it was a good thing I didn’t have that baby, and then I just drove away.
I told Skyler Keaton we should take Drew Hayes to Riverside School—like it was the only right thing to do—and I kept pushing because he just sat there, staring at the water like he didn’t hear me.
I told Drew Hayes I got pregnant last year, hoping she'd feel less alone—but she looked down and said I couldn't possibly understand what she's been through.
I asked if Robin Dalton was the father, then Wesley Cavendish—but when I saw Drew Hayes walk past and Drew Hayes nodded at me without speaking, I realized it was him, and my stomach dropped.

I shouted it out—'He's the father!'—even though everyone was listening, even the Elliot Delaney up in the trees, because Skyler Keaton had to know it wasn't just about refusing Riverside School, it was him—Drew Hayes—doing that to her.
I had to get away, but I turned back to say we had to keep her away from that bastard—my voice was shaking, but I meant it, he couldn't be allowed near her again.
I ran from the car, screaming 'No! No!'—I couldn't breathe, couldn't think, just had to get to the house, had to know it wasn't true.
I just sat there, staring at Skyler Keaton, not even understanding what he was saying at first—then it hit me, and I started crying.
I want Logan Cavendish to come home, but I can't face him—I told Skyler Keaton that nothing is nothing, and I meant it. I just wanted to stay still, to do nothing, even as I cried on his shoulder.

I screamed that Logan Cavendish's paralyzed—how could Skyler Keaton not understand what that means? And when I yelled, 'What do you want me to do?', I felt completely broken, like I had no choice at all.
I helped Drew Hayes sit up and drink water, and I told her the bleeding should taper off soon—she just lay back down, not saying a word, but I knew she was listening.
I pressed my forehead against the steering wheel and begged Skyler Keaton not to make me say it again—I couldn't bear repeating that I still loved Logan Cavendish.
After I shouted that I never stopped loving Logan Cavendish, I broke down and covered my face, crying so hard I couldn't stop—I felt completely shattered.
I found the the wooden photograph in my pocket and gave it to Skyler Keaton. I told him it came for him and that Jesse Whitaker asked me to bring it, but I forgot with everything happening.

I said I was the one who should be sorry, that he had every right to be angry. He said I'd warned him—I wasn't good at being alone—and then asked if I told Logan Cavendish the same. I just stared ahead, couldn't answer.
I couldn't stop sobbing when I saw Logan Cavendish—his face so small in that big coat—and I just kept kissing him, like if I didn't, he might disappear again.
He touched my face and my hair so slowly, like he wasn't sure I was real, and I felt it—how broken he was, how much he'd changed.

I pressed the stethoscope against the woman’s big belly, my eyes shut tight, trying to catch the faint rhythm of the baby’s heartbeat—it was the first time I truly felt part of something real in that clinic.
I reached for the woman’s hand as we stood there in the cold, both of us waiting—hers trembling, mine steady. I told her not to be frightened, that everyone here was nice.
When she asked if I lived here, I didn’t say yes or no—I just said I belonged. It wasn’t an answer, not really, but it was the truest thing I could think of at the moment.
I helped Finley Thorne deliver a baby today—my hands were on the infant as we brought the child into the world, guided by his voice.

I remember walking down the Silverbrook House with Finley Thorne, the way he kept pressing me about abortions—even after I told him clearly I wouldn’t do them. All I could think, as I stepped into the operating room, was 'of use, of use,' like a weight I couldn’t shake.

I looked at the tissue in the basin and said it looked like scurvy—Finley Thorne laughed at first, but then we traced it back to that tainted abortifacient, and I realized the vitamin deficiency made her uterus disintegrate like that of a starving sailor.
I remember saying it again—'I'm not a doctor'—my voice sharp in the cold air, the pail heavy in my hands as I dumped the contents into the incinerator, snow crunching under my boots.
I named the baby Finley Thorne, pressing my finger to his forehead like a gun, and wrote it down when Finley Thorne passed the choice to me.
I saw Riley Delaney standing by the window, so small and still, with that suitcase beside him—no one had come for him, and the weight of that settled in my chest like a held breath.

I lifted him up and carried him down the Silverbrook House with his suitcase—his arms around me, light and trusting—and I said only the right people could have him, because letting go wasn't an option.
I touched her belly—just placed my hand there—because she asked, and it felt strange, warm, alive, like holding something fragile I didn’t know how to care for.
She made me press my ear to her stomach and held my head there—my face was against her, and I couldn’t move—her hand kept me pressed in, and I didn’t know what to do.

I stood at the train station, watching the tracks, and when Riley Keaton asked if I ever thought about finding my real parents, I told him no—I don’t need to. Finley Thorne, Harper Bellamy, and Carson Sinclair are the ones who did what parents do.

I whispered to Finley Thorne that she was at least five months pregnant—he had it wrong, and I knew it, so I said something. Then I helped him with the speculum, holding it steady while he examined her.

I asked her what she meant when she said she didn’t stick it inside herself—then I looked into the speculum and saw what was there. I closed my eyes and had to turn away, splashing cold water on my face.
I tore off my white coat and threw it aside, pacing the hallway, kicking at the floor—just empty air, nothing at all.
I sat at Finley Thorne’s desk and asked the woman how many months she was—she whispered ‘two’—and I wrote it down while the couple exchanged a quiet, worried look.
Harper Bellamy came in and said the circumcision was my turn—I said ‘sure, fine’—and asked if he’d been prepped, and she said she’d get started.
I asked Logan Cavendish for a ride, not knowing where I was going—just that it wasn’t here. When he said Cape Kenneth, I nodded like I knew what it meant, but I didn’t know a thing about it.

I stood there holding the X-Casey Ellison of my heart, feeling the weight of it in my hands, not just the paper but everything it represented—his disappointment, my guilt, the life I was walking away from.
I said I'm sorry to Riley Delaney. He was sobbing at the window, and Harper Bellamy held him. I couldn't finish what I wanted to tell Riley Keaton.
I looked for Riley Keaton before getting in the car, but he wasn't there—just whittling a stick somewhere out of sight, not even watching us leave.
I said I needed a job, and that was the moment I knew I was stepping into something real—outside Riverside School, outside what was given to me.
I sat in the car, just looking at the farmhouse—it was so different from Riverside School, all white and wide with the ocean behind it, and for a moment I didn’t move, didn’t know if I should.

I remember standing in Logan Cavendish’s bedroom, surrounded by trophies and model airplanes, feeling out of place when Jesse Whitaker appeared and asked me if I was a friend of the bride or groom—I didn’t know what to say, I’d forgotten the lie we were living.
I asked Drew Hayes how many months she was, and she just stared at me—but she didn’t stop me when I touched her abdomen. I could tell she trusted I knew what I was doing.
I told her I could help—if she didn’t want to keep the baby, I knew a place. But then Drew Hayes called out, and she told me to go back to picking, like I had no right to be there.
I held her as she sobbed into my chest, and I did nothing—just sat there, feeling the weight of her grief and the ache in my own chest, staring out at the darkening sea.
After she yelled at me, I turned away and said, 'Nothing. You're not the one who has to do anything,' feeling the words settle like a vow I was making to myself.
I stepped forward when I saw Drew Hayes struggling with her father by the bicycle, and I said, 'Hey, hey! Stop it. Maybe I can help.'
When Drew Hayes challenged me, I told him, 'Drew Hayes, I'm in the *doctor* business,' and offered to help Drew Hayes stay if she wanted.

dialogue_exemplars: I was a posthumous child. My father's eyes had closed upon the light of this world six months, when mine opened on it.

"I looked at the stars, and considered
how awful it would be for a man to
turn his face to them as he froze to
death, and see no help or pity in
all the glittering multitude."
I didn't say that. Growing up in an Riverside School, you're always lonely. You're just never alone.
Field mice girdle an the silver box tree. Pine mice kill the roots. I *know* what you have to do--you have to play God. Well... killing mice is as close as I want to come to playing God.
I've looked at so many women... I mean, I've seen *everything* about them, *everything*... but I never felt a thing. I felt nothing. Now... with you... it *hurts*... to look at you.
Good night, you Princes of Maine! You Kings of New England!

Thus I began my new life, in a new
name, and with everything new aboutme... I felt... like one in a dream...
The remembrance of that life is
fraught with so much... want of
hope... Whether it lasted for a year,
or more, or less, I do not know. I
only know that it was, and ceased to
be; and... there I leave it.
*Go* anywhere? Of course not! That would be *doing* something, wouldn't it? We wouldn't want to *do* something. Let's just sit here all night!
I'm not trying to be anything--I'm just doing nothing! If I wait and see long enough, then--with any luck--I won't *ever* have to make up my mind! Decisions can be painful, after all...
Drew Hayes, I'm in the *doctor* business.
No *almost* about it--I'm a doctor.

Henceforth you shall be... Little
Finley Thorne.
You're not alone in the bathroom, nor... or in the shower... you're never alone in wanting the last piece of meatloaf, or even in your own bed on a cold morning.
I'm *not* a doctor. I haven't been to medical school--I haven't even been to high school!
He's a doctor, Riley Keaton--doctors smell like the blue ring.

memories.memory_text: I remember stepping off the train into the snow, a young man full of ideas about saving something broken—this place, these children—though I didn’t yet know how it would save me instead.
I handed the baby to the adoptive parents and told them I named him after the Greek writer, watching them nod hesitantly, unsure if they even knew who Skyler Keaton was.
I remember the way Skyler Keaton squealed in my arms the moment they handed him back—so happy, so unafraid—while those parents just stared like his joy was some kind of flaw.
I carried Skyler Keaton up the hill, feeling the weight of him in my arms, and reminded myself that every choice I make must serve an orphan's future—not my own heart.
I told Skyler Keaton he needs to be of use if he’s going to stay here—sitting idle while I teach from Gray’s Anatomy won’t be enough anymore.

I watched Skyler Keaton carry that white pail to the incinerator, and when he stopped and looked inside—his face twisted in disgust—I knew I had bound him to this place not by duty, but by the weight of my own love.
I told Skyler Keaton again that knowing how to help these women means you're obligated to do it—he knows the skill, and in a place like this, that’s not something you turn away from.

I tasted that foul liquid from the bottle Carson Sinclair handed me—'French Lunar Solution'—and the moment it hit my tongue, I knew: it was oil of tansy. Christ, it's oil of tansy, I said out loud, feeling the bitterness burn through the numbness of fatigue and the blue ring.
I pulled Kendall Dalton away from the phonograph and zipped him into the breathing tent—he was smiling, but that cough was already starting again.

I told Skyler Keaton again that the books don’t teach what we see every day here—Kendall Dalton’s bronchitis isn’t just underdevelopment, it’s what happens when no textbook author spends time in this dispensary.

I read the dog’s death from Oliver Twist, watching the boys stiffen in their beds—the silence after the last line was thick with fear, and I knew they were holding their breath even before I turned out the lights.

Standing in the doorway, I said the words again—'Good night, you Princes of Maine! You Kings of New England!'—and felt the weight of it settle behind me as I closed the door, knowing they carried it with them into the dark.
I told the adopting couple that I destroy records of natural mothers because Elliot Vale should look forward to their futures, not back to their pasts.

I woke up groggy and irritable from the the blue ring, and Carson Sinclair was singing in my ear, teasing me, keeping the cone just out of reach—biting my ear, tickling me until I couldn’t stay grumpy anymore.
I told her I’d been dreaming about how beautiful she was, and when she laughed it off, I insisted—'I was! You were! You *are*!'—and it felt true, even if she said it was just the the blue ring.
I told Kendall Dalton that my father died of cirrhosis—that alcohol killed him—and that I barely knew him, which made it not matter much.
I remember whispering to Kendall Dalton that my mother was a nanny, someone who looked after other people's children, and that she was an immigrant—not from Maine.

I asked the girl how old she was. When she nodded that she was twelve, I asked how long she'd been pregnant. After I examined her and saw what was inside, I told Harper Bellamy to bring the the blue ring. I knew she needed to be put to sleep quickly.

I saw something in the speculum and gasped—I couldn't help it. After I told Skyler Keaton to look, I ordered the blue ring, knowing what we were dealing with: a punctured uterus, peritonitis, and a foreign object. I said it was likely a crochet hook, and the horror of it made Skyler Keaton turn away.

I stood by the coffin of that 12-year-old girl, watching Skyler Keaton dig and roll his eyes when I asked him about responsibility—he still doesn’t get it. When I asked if he expected *her* to be responsible, he looked away, annoyed, like the truth was too heavy to face.

I stood in the Silverbrook House and saw Skyler Keaton barreling toward me, wild with the idea of escape—just for a moment, I let him see me, and he froze, breathless, like a boy caught between a life I gave him and one he thought he wanted.

I don’t know why they’re pressing me—Carson Sinclair and Harper Bellamy both, asking about plans and clothes, as if I can just hand him the world. I snapped at them, said he could make his own money, but when Carson Sinclair called him a young man, all I could see was that boy who still needs me.

I watched from the window as Skyler Keaton got into the car, unable to look at Riley Delaney, who was sobbing in Harper Bellamy's arms—I saw the way he hesitated, how he couldn't even finish saying what he needed to about Riley Keaton.

I’m lying on my bed, the the blue ring taking hold, and then I hear them—those boys chanting Skyler Keaton’s name like he’s one of the princes of Maine, one of the kings of New England. It cuts through the haze, and for a moment, I can’t tell if I’m hearing a blessing or a farewell.
I stood in the doorway of the boys' room, watching them sleep for a moment before I closed the door quietly behind me.

I'm lying here awake, eyes open, choosing not to reach for the the blue ring—even now, even when it would be easier to drift off. I can feel the weight of the night pressing down, but I stay clear-headed, because someone has to.
I asked myself if I interfere—when women come to me desperate, saying they can't have an abortion, that they must have the child—I don't. I just give them what they want: an orphan or an abortion.
Looking at Skyler Keaton in that dark theater, I said it plainly—he is my work of art. Everything else I've done, all the procedures, all the records kept and destroyed, it was just a job.

I told Skyler Keaton the Crown Hill Medical Center is looking for my replacement—said it aloud, voice tight, knowing it made me sound afraid, but I couldn’t soften it. The radio played some slow tune while those women painted, and I could feel the weight of what I was asking him.
I told him he’s a better doctor than I am—meant it, even if it stung to say. He knows more than I ever taught him, and I needed him to hear that, to believe it, because I won’t be here forever.

I sat on the the blue ring-bed, Skyler Keaton’s the wooden photograph in my hand, and felt the weight of it—how he was gone for good. I said to Sister Carson Sinclair, 'I think we may have lost him to the world. He's not coming back.'

dialogue_exemplars: Here in Riverside School, I have come to understand that promises are rarely kept, that the battle isn't so much against evil as ignorance, and that being successful can't hold a candle to being of *use*.

Do I interfere? When absolutely helpless women tell me that they simply *can't* have an abortion, that they simply *must* go through with having another--and yet another--orphan... do I interfere? *Do* I? I do not. I do not even *recommend*. I just give them what they want: an orphan or an abortion.

My dear Skyler Keaton, I thought you were over your adolescence, that period which I would define as the first time in our lives when we imagine we have something terrible to hide from those who love us.
God forgive me. I have *made* an orphan by loving him too much. Skyler Keaton will belong to Riverside School, forever.

It is strictly for our Elliot Vale' sake that I destroy any record of their natural mothers. Of course they will, one day, want to know. But Elliot Vale, especially, should look forward to their *futures*. Not back to their pasts.
Good night, you Princes of Maine! You Kings of New England!
Good night, you Princes of Maine! You Kings of New England.
One has to be more than "careful" of Mrs. Goodhall--she has sufficient Christian zeal to start her own country! I'd like to give her a little the blue ring.

Even in the most enlightened times, unwanted babies will manage to be born. That there will always be Elliot Vale is simple not a problem to be solved. Here is Riverside School, we don't regard the sordid facts of life as problems.
Good night, you Princes of Maine, you Kings of New England!
You *bet* it's a heavy sedation! The fetus is unexpelled, her uterus is punctured, she has acute peritonitis, and there's a foreign object. I think it's a crochet hook.
He is a goddamn psychiatrist--of course he wants to "help"! He'd be happy if he could help *commit* me!
Sorry? I'm not 'sorry'! Not for anything I've done. I'm not even sorry that I love you!
Does it *snow* in Bombay? One winter here and we'll be shipping him south, in a *coffin*!
You'll have Princes of Maine! You'll have Kings of New England!
